'''Thomas J. Kelly''' is an American cancer researcher whose work focuses on the molecular mechanisms of [[DNA replication]]. Kelly is  director of the Sloan-Kettering Institute,<ref name="Johns Hopkins Malaria Research">{{cite web | title=Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute External Advisory Board| url=http://malaria.jhsph.edu/people/external_advisory_board |access-date=February 28, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Director of the Institute for Basic Biomedical Sciences">{{cite web | title=NIH Director Welcomes Five New Members to the Advisory Committee to the Director |url=http://www.nih.gov/news/health/jan2008/od-31.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081001153809/http://www.nih.gov/news/health/jan2008/od-31.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 1, 2008 | publisher=National Institutes of Health |date=January 31, 2008}}</ref> the basic research arm of the [[Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center]]. He holds the Center's [[Benno C. Schmidt, Sr.|Benno C. Schmidt]] Chair of Cancer Research.

Before joining Sloan-Kettering in 2002, Kelly was professor and director of the Department of Molecular Biology<ref name="Oxford Journal">{{cite journal|title=Awards, Appointments, Announcements|journal=Journal of the National Cancer Institute|year=2002|volume=94|issue=3|pages=165–166|doi=10.1093/jnci/94.3.165|url=http://jnci.oxfordjournals.org/content/94/3/165.full#sec-3}}</ref>  and Genetics at the [[Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine]] and was the founding director of the Johns Hopkins Institute for Basic Biomedical Sciences.<ref name="Director of the Institute for Basic Biomedical Sciences"/><ref name="The New York Times Article">{{cite news|title=Kari Evans, Mark Kelly Wedding Announcement | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/11/fashion/weddings/11kevans.html | work=The New York Times  | date=2007-11-11}}</ref>

Kelly pioneered the study of DNA replication in [[eukaryote|eukaryotic]] cells by using DNA viruses as model systems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kelly, Thomas J., Brown, Grant W.|title=Regulation of Chromosome Replication|journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry|volume=69|pages=829–880|doi=10.1146/annurev.biochem.69.1.829|pmid=10966477|date=July 2000}}</ref>  His laboratory developed the first cell-free systems for studying the biochemistry of DNA replication in [[human cell]]s, enabling the identification and functional characterization of components of the human replication machinery.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Thomas J. |last1=Kelly |first2=Bruce |last2=Stillman |year=2006 |chapter=Duplication of DNA in Eukaryotic Cells |chapter-url=https://www.cshlpress.com/pdf/sample/dnarep.pdf |editor1-first=Melvin L |editor1-last=DePamphilis |title=DNA Replication and Human Disease |pages=1–29 |publisher=Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press |location=Cold Spring Harbor, New York |isbn=978-0-87969-766-2}}
</ref>

In recognition of this work he received the 2004 [[Alfred P. Sloan, Jr. Prize]] of the General Motors Cancer Research Foundation<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.landesbioscience.com/journals/cbt/article/1049/?nocache=607349094 |title=2004 Alfred P. Sloan Jr. Prize of the General Motors Cancer Research Foundation |publisher=Landesbioscience.com |date=1979-05-02 |access-date=2013-04-23}}</ref> and the 2010 [[Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize]] of [[Columbia University]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://ps.columbia.edu/news/honoring-two-pioneers-genetics-and-cancer-research | title=Honoring Two Pioneers of Genetics and Cancer Research | publisher=Columbia University | date=2011-02-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.cumc.columbia.edu/faculty/vice-dean/horwitz-prize/prize-awardees | title=The Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize for Biology or Biochemistry |publisher= Columbia University Medical Center | access-date=2013-03-05}}</ref>

==Career==
Kelly earned a [[Ph.D.]] in [[biophysics]] in 1968<ref>{{cite web | url=http://biophysics.jhu.edu/alumni.html | title=Department of Biophysics Alumni | year=1968}}</ref> and an [[M.D.]] in 1969.{{citation needed|date=May 2015}} While a postdoctoral fellow with [[Hamilton O. Smith]] at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine during 1969-70,<ref>[http://archive.gazette.jhu.edu/2010/05/24/society-of-scholars-inducts-new-members/ Thomas J. Kelly Jr., New York], Retrieved on March 5, 2013</ref>  Kelly determined the DNA sequences recognized by type II restriction enzymes, which subsequently became major tools in recombinant DNA research.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(70)90150-6 |title=A restriction enzyme from ''Hemophilus influenzae'': II. Base sequence of the recognition site |year=1970 |last1=Kelly |first1=Thomas J. |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=393–409 |pmid=5312501 |last2=Smith |first2=Hamilton O.}}</ref> In 1970 he moved to the [[National Institutes of Health]] as a member of the [[United States Public Health Service]] and conducted research on the [[DNA viruses]], [[adenovirus]] and [[SV40]], which cause tumors in animals.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Simian virus 40 integration site in an adenovirus 7-simian virus 40 hybrid DNA molecule|year=1971 |last1=Kelly |first1=T J |last2=Rose |first2=J A |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=68 |issue=5 |pages=1037–41 |doi=10.1073/pnas.68.5.1037|pmid=4324999 |bibcode=1971PNAS...68.1037K |pmc=389108 |doi-access=free }}</ref> He joined the faculty in the Department of Microbiology at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in 1972, where he began to exploit viruses as potentially powerful model systems for exploring the mechanisms of DNA replication in human cells.<ref name="NIH SMRB">{{cite web|title= NIH, Scientific Management Review Board, Thomas Kelly, M.D., Ph.D.|url=http://smrb.od.nih.gov/bios/tkelly |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111015184218/http://smrb.od.nih.gov/bios/tkelly |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 15, 2011 }}U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, March 4, 2013</ref>

Using proteins derived from human cells, he and his colleagues developed the first cell-free DNA replication systems capable of duplicating the complete genomes of adenovirus and SV40.<ref>{{Cite journal|vauthors=Kelly TJ, Rosenfeld PJ, Wides RJ, O'Neill EA, Li JJ, Wold MS |title=Replication of adenovirus and SV40 chromosomes in vitro|pmid=2894680|journal=Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. B|volume=317|issue=1187|pages=429–438|doi=10.1098/rstb.1987.0070|date=December 15, 1987|bibcode=1987RSPTB.317..429K|doi-access=}}</ref> The SV40 system proved to be a particularly useful system because SV40 relies largely on the cellular replication machinery for the duplication of its genome. Thus, biochemical analysis of the SV40 system made it possible to identify and functionally characterize proteins and enzymes that carry out the duplication of the chromosomal DNA in human cells.<ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=http://www.charitywire.com/charity95/03577.html | title=New Leadership at Memorial Sloan-Kettering | publisher=Charity Wire |chapter=Article 03577 | date=2001-12-26}}</ref> In subsequent work Kelly and colleagues have shifted their focus from studying the machinery of DNA replication to the mechanism that controls it.  Studying these mechanisms are essential for ensuring the accuracy of DNA replication during the cell cycle in human cells and in fission yeast ([[Schizosaccharomyces pombe]]), which is highly significant in understanding cancer.<ref name="Molecular Biology">{{cite web|title=Sloan-Kettering Institute, Molecular Biology, Thomas J. Kelly|url=http://www2.mskcc.org/mskcc/html/12507.cfm?Gerstner_Title=Thomas%20J.%20Kelly&Gerstner_URL=http%3A//www2.mskcc.org/gerstner/html/55785.cfm|publisher=Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center|access-date=14 March 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Brush, GeorgeS., Anderson, Carl W., and Kelly, Thomas J.|title=The DNA-activated protein kinase is required for the phosphorylation of replication protein A during simian virus 40 DNA replication|journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA|volume=91|issue=26|pages=12520–12524|url=http://www.pnas.org/content/91/26/12520.full.pdf|access-date=March 8, 2013|date=December 1994|doi=10.1073/pnas.91.26.12520|pmid=7809070|pmc=45470|bibcode=1994PNAS...9112520B|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Brown, Grant W. |author2=Kelly, Thomas J. |name-list-style=amp |title=Cell cycle regulation of Dfp1, an activator of the Hsk1|journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA |date=July 1999 |volume=96|issue=15 |pages=8443–8448|url=http://www.pnas.org/content/96/15/8443.full.pdf|doi=10.1073/pnas.96.15.8443|pmid=10411894|pmc=17535|bibcode=1999PNAS...96.8443B|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Since 2002, Kelly has been the director of the Sloan-Kettering Institute, where he has expanded or re-invigorated some of its laboratory research programs.<ref name="Society of Scholars">{{cite news | url=http://issuu.com/johnshopkins/docs/24may_issue__all_pages_?mode=window&pageNumber=1 | title=The JHU Gazette - May 24, 2010 |publisher=Issuu.com | page=12 |date=2010-05-24 |access-date=2012-06-05}}</ref> Kelly also led the establishment of the Gerstner Sloan-Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, which provides a novel curriculum in basic and translational cancer biology leading to the Ph.D. degree.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.newswise.com/articles/memorial-sloan-kettering-cancer-center-starts-new-graduate-school | title=Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center Starts New Graduate School | publisher=Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center | date=2005-07-26}}</ref><ref>[http://www2.mskcc.org/gerstner/html/55785.cfm Gerstner Sloan-Kettering Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences Thomas J. Kelly's Welcome], Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, Retrieved on March 5, 2013</ref>
